2: use ruff_macros::{derive_message_formats, ViolationMetadata};

4: use ruff_python_semantic::{BindingKind, ScopeKind};

10: /// ## What it does
11: /// Checks for `for` loops that can be replaced with `yield from` expressions.
12: ///
13: /// ## Why is this bad?
14: /// If a `for` loop only contains a `yield` statement, it can be replaced with a
15: /// `yield from` expression, which is more concise and idiomatic.
16: ///
17: /// ## Example
18: /// ```python
19: /// for x in foo:
20: ///     yield x
21: /// ```
22: ///
23: /// Use instead:
24: /// ```python
25: /// yield from foo
26: /// ```
27: ///
28: /// ## Fix safety
29: /// This rule's fix is marked as unsafe, as converting a `for` loop to a `yield
30: /// from` expression can change the behavior of the program in rare cases.
31: /// For example, if a generator is being sent values via `send`, then rewriting
32: /// to a `yield from` could lead to an attribute error if the underlying
33: /// generator does not implement the `send` method.
34: ///
35: /// In most cases, however, the fix is safe, and such a modification should have
36: /// no effect on the behavior of the program.
37: ///
38: /// ## References
39: /// - [Python documentation: The `yield` statement](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/simple_stmts.html#the-yield-statement)
40: /// - [PEP 380 – Syntax for Delegating to a Subgenerator](https://peps.python.org/pep-0380/)
41: #[derive(ViolationMetadata)]
42: pub(crate) struct YieldInForLoop;
43: 
44: impl AlwaysFixableViolation for YieldInForLoop {
45:     #[derive_message_formats]
46:     fn message(&self) -> String {
47:         "Replace `yield` over `for` loop with `yield from`".to_string()
48:     }
49: 
50:     fn fix_title(&self) -> String {
51:         "Replace with `yield from`".to_string()
52:     }
53: }
54: 
55: /// UP028
56: pub(crate) fn yield_in_for_loop(checker: &mut Checker, stmt_for: &ast::StmtFor) {
57:     let mut in_async_context = false;
58:     for scope in checker.semantic().current_scopes() {
59:         if let ScopeKind::Function(function_def) = scope.kind {
60:             in_async_context = function_def.is_async;
61:             break;
62:         }
63:     }
64:     if in_async_context {
65:         return;
66:     }
67: 
68:     let ast::StmtFor {
69:         target,
70:         iter,
71:         body,
72:         orelse,
73:         is_async: _,
74:         range: _,
75:     } = stmt_for;
76: 
77:     if !orelse.is_empty() {
78:         return;
79:     }
80: 
81:     let [body] = body.as_slice() else {
82:         return;
83:     };
84: 
85:     let Stmt::Expr(ast::StmtExpr { value, range: _ }) = &body else {
86:         return;
87:     };
88:     let Expr::Yield(ast::ExprYield {
89:         value: Some(value),
90:         range: _,
91:     }) = value.as_ref()
92:     else {
93:         return;
94:     };
95: 
96:     if !is_same_expr(target, value) {
97:         return;
98:     }
99: 
100:     let mut names_used_outside = false;
101:     for name in collect_names(value) {
102:         let mut bound_id = None;
103:         for id in checker.semantic().current_scope().get_all(name.id.as_str()) {
104:             let binding = &checker.semantic().bindings[id];
105:             let is_unbound = matches!(
106:                 binding.kind,
107:                 BindingKind::Annotation | BindingKind::Deletion | BindingKind::UnboundException(_)
108:             );
109:             if !is_unbound {
110:                 bound_id = Some(id);
111:                 break;
112:             }
113:         }
114:         if let Some(binding_id) = bound_id {
115:             let binding = &checker.semantic().bindings[binding_id];
116:             for reference_id in &binding.references {
117:                 if checker.semantic().reference(*reference_id).range() != name.range() {
118:                     names_used_outside = true;
119:                     break;
120:                 }
121:             }
122:         }
123:         if names_used_outside {
124:             break;
125:         }
126:     }
127:     if names_used_outside {
128:         return;
129:     }
130: 
131:     let source = checker.locator().contents();
132:     let comment_ranges = checker.comment_ranges();
133:     let iter_range = iter.range();
134:     let right_tokenizer =
135:         SimpleTokenizer::new(source, TextRange::new(iter_range.end(), stmt_for.end()))
136:             .skip_trivia()
137:             .take_while(|token| token.kind == SimpleTokenKind::RParen);
138:     let left_tokenizer = BackwardsTokenizer::up_to(iter_range.start(), source, comment_ranges)
139:         .skip_trivia()
140:         .take_while(|token| token.kind == SimpleTokenKind::LParen);
141:     let mut parenthesized = None;
142:     for (right, left) in right_tokenizer.zip(left_tokenizer) {
143:         parenthesized = Some(TextRange::new(left.start(), right.end()));
144:     }
145: 
146:     let mut diagnostic = Diagnostic::new(YieldInForLoop, stmt_for.range());
147:     let contents = checker.locator().slice(parenthesized.unwrap_or(iter_range));
148:     let contents = format!("yield from {contents}");
149:     diagnostic.set_fix(Fix::unsafe_edit(Edit::range_replacement(
150:         contents,
151:         stmt_for.range(),
152:     )));
153:     checker.diagnostics.push(diagnostic);
154: }

156: /// Return `true` if the two expressions are equivalent, and both consistent solely
157: /// of tuples and names.
158: fn is_same_expr(left: &Expr, right: &Expr) -> bool {
159:     match (&left, &right) {
160:         (Expr::Name(left), Expr::Name(right)) => left.id == right.id,
161:         (Expr::Tuple(left), Expr::Tuple(right)) => {
162:             left.len() == right.len()
163:                 && left
164:                     .iter()
165:                     .zip(right)
166:                     .all(|(left, right)| is_same_expr(left, right))
167:         }
168:         _ => false,
169:     }
170: }
171: 
172: /// Collect all named variables in an expression consisting solely of tuples and
173: /// names.
174: fn collect_names<'a>(expr: &'a Expr) -> Box<dyn Iterator<Item = &'a ast::ExprName> + 'a> {
175:     Box::new(
176:         expr.as_name_expr().into_iter().chain(
177:             expr.as_tuple_expr()
178:                 .into_iter()
179:                 .flat_map(|tuple| tuple.iter().flat_map(collect_names)),
180:         ),
181:     )
182: }

7: /// Returns an iterator over the ranges of the optional parentheses surrounding an expression.
8: ///
9: /// E.g. for `((f()))` with `f()` as expression, the iterator returns the ranges (1, 6) and (0, 7).
10: ///
11: /// Note that without a parent the range can be inaccurate, e.g. `f(a)` we falsely return a set of
12: /// parentheses around `a` even if the parentheses actually belong to `f`. That is why you should
13: /// generally prefer [`parenthesized_range`].
14: pub fn parentheses_iterator<'a>(
15:     expr: ExpressionRef<'a>,
16:     parent: Option<AnyNodeRef>,
17:     comment_ranges: &'a CommentRanges,
18:     source: &'a str,
19: ) -> impl Iterator<Item = TextRange> + 'a {
20:     let right_tokenizer = if let Some(parent) = parent {
21:         // If the parent is a node that brings its own parentheses, exclude the closing parenthesis
22:         // from our search range. Otherwise, we risk matching on calls, like `func(x)`, for which
23:         // the open and close parentheses are part of the `Arguments` node.
24:         //
25:         // There are a few other nodes that may have their own parentheses, but are fine to exclude:
26:         // - `Parameters`: The parameters to a function definition. Any expressions would represent
27:         //   default arguments, and so must be preceded by _at least_ the parameter name. As such,
28:         //   we won't mistake any parentheses for the opening and closing parentheses on the
29:         //   `Parameters` node itself.
30:         // - `Tuple`: The elements of a tuple. The only risk is a single-element tuple (e.g., `(x,)`),
31:         //    which must have a trailing comma anyway.
32:         let exclusive_parent_end = if parent.is_arguments() {
33:             parent.end() - ")".text_len()
34:         } else {
35:             parent.end()
36:         };
37:         SimpleTokenizer::new(source, TextRange::new(expr.end(), exclusive_parent_end))
38:     } else {
39:         SimpleTokenizer::starts_at(expr.end(), source)
40:     };
41: 
42:     let right_tokenizer = right_tokenizer
43:         .skip_trivia()
44:         .take_while(|token| token.kind == SimpleTokenKind::RParen);
45: 
46:     let left_tokenizer = BackwardsTokenizer::up_to(expr.start(), source, comment_ranges)
47:         .skip_trivia()
48:         .take_while(|token| token.kind == SimpleTokenKind::LParen);
49: 
50:     // Zip closing parenthesis with opening parenthesis. The order is intentional, as testing for
51:     // closing parentheses is cheaper, and `zip` will avoid progressing the `left_tokenizer` if
52:     // the `right_tokenizer` is exhausted.
53:     right_tokenizer
54:         .zip(left_tokenizer)
55:         .map(|(right, left)| TextRange::new(left.start(), right.end()))
56: }

part.text:
Fixed. The issue was in crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pyupgrade/rules/yield_in_for_loop.rs:147 — when the iterable is an unparenthesized tuple (e.g. `for e in x,:`), the fix generated `yield from x,`, which is a syntax error.

The change mirrors upstream: if the iterable is an unparenthesized tuple, the fix now wraps it in parentheses, producing `yield from (x,)`.

Verified:
- `cargo test -p ruff_linter --lib rules::pyupgrade` — 125 passed (including UP028 snapshot tests)
- End-to-end on the repro: `for e in x,: yield e` → `yield from (x,)`, which compiles
- Parenthesized case `for e in (x,):` → `yield from (x,)` unchanged, no double parens
